title: Indian Scientists Pinpoint Martian Analogue Sites, Boosting Planetary Research Prospects
body:
Kerala‑based geologists have pinpointed two terrestrial locales that closely mimic the mineralogical and environmental conditions of ancient Mars, a discovery that could sharpen the search for the Red Planet’s lost water and potential biosignatures. By detecting hydrous sulfate deposits in Tamil Nadu’s arid hinterlands and in Chile’s Atacama Desert, the research team has highlighted sites where Mars‑like chemistry, climate history and surface processes converge, offering a natural laboratory for planetary scientists worldwide.

The study, led by Dr. Anjali Menon of the Centre for Earth Sciences at the University of Kerala, focused on the presence of magnesium‑rich sulfates such as epsomite (MgSO₄·7H₂O) and kieserite (MgSO₄·H₂O). These minerals form under conditions of evaporative concentration and periodic wetting–drying cycles—processes that are thought to have sculpted large swathes of the Martian crust during the planet’s Noachian and Hesperian epochs. “When we examined the spectral signatures of these sulfates in the field, they matched the orbital data from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s CRISM instrument almost perfectly,” Dr. Menon explained. “It suggests that the same geochemical pathways that produced these salts on Earth could have operated on Mars billions of years ago.”

In Tamil Nadu, the researchers surveyed the dry lake beds of the Kaveri basin, where ancient playa deposits have been intermittently flooded by monsoonal runoff. The region’s hyper‑arid microclimate, combined with high rates of evaporation, has led to the precipitation of layered sulfate crusts that preserve fine‑scale sedimentary structures. These formations bear striking resemblance to the stratified sulfate deposits observed in the Meridiani Planum region of Mars, where the rover Opportunity famously uncovered hematite-rich spherules. Laboratory analyses of the Tamil Nadu samples revealed micro‑textures indicative of periodic brine activity, a key factor in assessing habitability potential.

Across the Pacific, the Atacama Desert—already renowned as the most Mars‑like terrain on Earth—provided a complementary analogue. The team drilled into the hyper‑arid core of the Yungay basin, uncovering subsurface horizons enriched with hydrated magnesium sulfates that have persisted for millennia under relentless ultraviolet radiation and extreme diurnal temperature swings. “The Atacama’s preservation of hydrated minerals despite its hostile surface conditions mirrors what we expect on Mars, where subsurface niches could shield delicate biosignatures from harsh radiation,” noted co‑author Dr. Luis Alvarez of the Chilean Institute of Planetary Sciences.

Beyond the mineralogical parallels, the two sites share a suite of physical characteristics that enhance their analogue value. Both exhibit low atmospheric pressure analogues (simulated in laboratory chambers), high salt concentrations, and limited organic carbon—conditions that constrain microbial life to extremophilic niches. By conducting in‑situ experiments, such as inoculating the sulfate layers with terrestrial halophiles, scientists can test the survivability of life under Mars‑like stresses. Early trials have already demonstrated that certain archaea can remain metabolically active within the crystal lattices of epsomite, hinting at possible pathways for fossil preservation on Mars.

The implications of this discovery extend to upcoming planetary missions. NASA’s Perseverance rover, currently exploring Jezero Crater, and the European Space Agency’s Rosalind Franklin rover, slated for launch later this decade, will rely heavily on Earth analogues to calibrate instruments and interpret data. The Kerala team’s findings provide concrete field sites where rover payloads—such as Raman spectrometers, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) tools, and subsurface drills—can be tested under realistic conditions before deployment. Moreover, the identified analogues could serve as staging grounds for international collaborative experiments, fostering a shared framework for planetary protection protocols.

Looking ahead, the researchers plan to map additional sulfate‑rich zones across the Indian subcontinent and to expand their comparative study to include basaltic terrains that host iron‑bearing minerals akin to those on Mars. By integrating remote sensing, geochemical modeling, and microbiological assays, the initiative aims to build a comprehensive analogue database that will sharpen the search for ancient Martian habitability. As humanity prepares for the next wave of robotic explorers and, eventually, crewed missions, these Earth‑based windows into Mars’ past may prove pivotal in unraveling the Red Planet’s most enduring mystery: whether it ever harbored life.
